slides.text: As an archivist for rare books, Maya loved the marginalia most of all—the scribbled thoughts left behind in the borders of forgotten novels by readers long dead. In a battered 1912 edition of Keats purchased at an estate sale in Edinburgh, she found handwritten pencil notes in the margins: 'To my dearest Leo—these lines are the only way I know how to stay beside you.' The handwriting was delicate, fierce, signed only with the initial 'C.'

Seven years later, while cataloging an entirely unrelated volume of Rainer Maria Rilke at an auction in Montreal, Maya’s breath hitched. In the margins of page forty-four, written in that exact same distinctive, flowing cursive, was another note: 'Leo, fifty years have passed since Edinburgh. I still search for your handwriting in every bookshop between here and the sea. If you ever hold this book, know that I never loved anyone else.'

Maya checked the provenance registry of the Montreal auction house to trace the book’s donor. The consignor was an eighty-nine-year-old retired astronomer named Leo Bennett. Maya bought a train ticket that very afternoon, knocked on his door in Old Quebec, and placed the Edinburgh Keats alongside the Montreal Rilke on his kitchen table. The old man touched the two book covers with trembling hands, closed his eyes, and whispered, 'She found me. After all these years, she found me.'
